primers.lede: Your first plates teach heat, the knife and the pan a few techniques at a time, and every one of them should go up without notes.
paragraphs: Most of the dishes placed at Commis come from the opening semesters of the Path of Study, and the library rates nearly all of them Easy. Each rests on techniques from your first weeks, and a couple of runs should put it in your hands.

Start where the Path starts, with Knife & Fire Foundations, and take The French Omelette first. It is eight minutes of heat control, seasoning and pan work, and the library rates it a step harder than the rest here, so cook it until the heat stops surprising you. Ratatouille is the knife-cut dish: dice, julienne and bias, then the sauté. Chicken Piccata strings four moves onto one plate: the dredge, the sear, the deglaze and a reduced pan sauce. Salade Niçoise asks for blanching and shocking, so what you blanch keeps its color and stops cooking the moment it hits the ice.

Then the simmer. Miso Soup teaches dashi and soaking dried goods back to life, and the semester asks for dashi's restraint and for watching the bubble, not the clock. Pasta e Fagioli teaches sweating aromatics, soft and never browned, which is the onion's patience in a single pot.

The sauté station follows, the semester the Path calls the line cook's exam. Shrimp Scampi repeats the piccata's sear and deglaze on something that cooks in moments, so pull it once it turns opaque. Chicken Teriyaki is about resting the meat and slicing against the grain before it reaches the plate. Garides Saganaki sweats its aromatics, takes a flambé and keeps its cooking liquid.

Panna Cotta sits in Pastry Fundamentals, later on the Path, but the library rates it Easy and its techniques are small ones: the liquid held at a bare simmer below the boil, passed through a sieve, and the set judged by the wobble. Cook it whenever you want a dessert on the log.

A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged, and nothing more is asked of it. Use the Read the semester door to open the Path at the semester that teaches the first dish you have not yet cooked, Cook the next dish to go straight to its recipe page, and The library at this level for the full grid of Easy plates. The Level test at the foot of the page runs across every subsection, untimed, and hands back what you missed with the right answers.
primers.next: Chef de Partie moves into the middle semesters and the library's Intermediate plates: the braise in Boeuf Bourguignon and Coq au Vin, bread in Rosemary Focaccia, custard in Crème Brûlée, and fish at the sauté station in Sole Meunière.

primers.lede: The techniques a station runs on all day: the cuts, salted water, the sweat, the sear, the simmer, and the pan you never wash before it has made its sauce.
paragraphs: Take the board first. Knife cuts sit on more recipes than almost anything else here, and the standard is uniformity, not speed: any three pieces should match. Then the pot. Salted water & the float test, blanching & shocking and the bare simmer are one lesson at two heats, the rolling boil and the shiver under it: water seasoned before anything goes in, an ice bath ready before the timer starts, a surface watched rather than set once. Skimming and keeping the cooking liquid come after: lift the foam, hold it below the boil, save the liquid.

The pan is one lesson with three heats. Sweating aromatics is low heat and no color. Sautéing & the shallow fry is a single layer kept moving, light color fast. Searing is the hard crust: a pan that never falls quiet and a piece that releases itself. A recipe that says cook the onions means one of the three; learn which before the rest of the pan. Deglazing & pan sauces, reducing a sauce and making a roux follow: the fond brown and not black, salt at the end because it concentrates, the roux taken to its stage and no further.

Roasting in a hot oven, the broiler and charring over open flame are dry heat from three directions: all around, from above, and straight against the surface. Each has its marks: the oven fully up to heat and air around every piece; the broiler lit first and somebody standing at it, because pale turns bitter in tens of seconds; nothing between flame and surface, no acrid edge. Griddle & plancha work and tortillas on the comal want full contact with dry metal. Resting meat & slicing against the grain closes the roast: off before the target, a dry board when you cut. The fryer is a chain in order: the coat before the fry, deep frying at temperature, draining fried food on a rack, salted within seconds.

Salt, cold, time and hands come next. Salting to draw the water out is salt on every face, somewhere for the water to go, and that water poured off before heat; brining & curing is full commitment, timed against weight and thickness, dried before anything crisps. Chilling to firm and the overnight rest are waiting done properly: cooled fast first, cold through, not cold at the rim. Shaping by hand, whipping a meringue and the wobble & the skewer belong to the bake: matched pieces with sealed seams, stiff peaks with a slight bow, a skewer tested at the true center. Caramelizing onions, brown butter, poaching eggs, trussing, flambé and sourdough starter carry no written standard.

Eight more carry their own marks. Soaking dried goods back to life is tested at the center of the largest piece; steaming is the lid left on over a rolling boil; straining & passing through a sieve and mashing & puréeing are judged on the tongue; dashi is pale gold and clear, kombu out before the first bubbles. Frying the paste until the oil splits, dry-pan toasting and egg wash & the baker's shine each have one signal: clear fat pooling at the edges, fragrance before color, a thin even coat with nothing pooled.

Met has one rule. A technique with a written standard is met when a cook on one of its recipes was graded met against that standard; one without a standard is met by any cook of one of its recipes. Open Read the techniques and work down the index in the order above, the last eight as their recipes come up. Open The next technique between services: the page of the first technique not yet met.

primers.lede: At Commis the Lexicon is the words the pass will use on you: the prep and pan verbs, the staples, and how to taste.
paragraphs: Start with the words the first semesters lean on, because the rest of the level hangs on them. Mise en Place is the habit before the skill: read the recipe fully, prep completely, then light the burner. Knife Cuts: The Classical Ladder gives you brunoise, julienne, batonnet and the dice, and uniformity is the exam: speed comes later. Then the pan verbs. Sweat vs. Sauté vs. Sear separates three different flavors that a recipe may lump together as cooking the onions, and Deglaze & Fond turns the browned layer left in the pan into the base of a sauce.

Take the heat words next, as one family, since each is a decision about temperature. Poach, Simmer, Boil teaches you to watch the bubbles, not the dial. Blanch & Shock is brief boiling in heavily salted water, then an ice bath, the move that lets a short service plate a long mise. Three entries build the sauce corner, taken in this order: Stocks; Roux, Slurry & Liaison; then Reduction, Nappe & Mounting. Skim the stock and never salt it, pick the thickener for the heat the sauce will see next, and reduce before you season. Searing & Pan Technique and Resting, Carryover & the Thermometer close the set: dry the protein, never crowd the pan, cook to temp and not to time.

The produce and staples are the words on your board from day one. Allium Family, Yellow Onion and Garlic explain why the size of the cut sets the pungency, and why garlic goes in after the onions, off the fiercest heat. Mirepoix, Trinity, Sofrito & Friends names the aromatic bases that open cuisine after cuisine. Starchy vs. Waxy Potatoes tells you to match the potato to the job before the recipe, and Hearty vs. Tender Herbs tells you when each goes in: rosemary and thyme early, basil and parsley at the end. The rest, such as the fruit and vegetable atlases, cuts like Chuck and pans like Cast Iron and Stainless Clad (Tri-Ply), read best as they land on your prep list, not front to back.

Keep one group open for the whole level: Tasting & Seasoning Like a Chef, Salt & Perception and The Repair Table. Taste at every stage and season in layers. The Palate on this page puts the repair table's first two faults on a plate, lever by lever; here you learn the words your chef will use at the pass when a plate comes back.

Use the doors in order. Read the terms opens the Lexicon at this level, and Flashcards and Quiz then run over the same words. A term is met once your recall of it is marked met or close on the flashcard ladder, or in the quiz; a miss alone is never met.

cites.name: The Repair Table: Balancing a Dish

primers.lede: The Floor Deck at Commis is the menu words a guest will ask about tonight, taken by method first, then the cuts, the fish case and the larder.
paragraphs: These are the deck's first cards, one to a menu word. Each card gives a gist, a why and a menu line, and most give the thing it is not. Read the line first, the way the word reaches you on the floor, then the not-this where the card has one: that is what a guest will confuse it with.

Take the twenty methods first; every other card leans on them. Boiled, Simmered and Poached are one ladder of heat in liquid, from a rolling bubble to none at all, and Steamed sits above the water, not in it. Seared, Sautéed, Fried and Grilled are the dry, hot, fast side, with Blackened and Chicken-Fried as two Southern turns in a skillet. Braised is the slow one, half in liquid under a lid; Roasted is the oven's dry heat, fast or slow. Brined, Cured and Pickled happen to food before or instead of cooking; Smoked either flavors it cold or cooks it low and slow. Learn each by the neighbor it is set against: Simmered is not Boiled, Seared is not Caramelized, Cured is not Smoked.

Bacon, Prosciutto, Pastrami, Corned Beef and Chorizo tie straight back to Brined, Cured and Smoked, so take them while those cards are fresh. Then the block: the steakhouse cuts run from Tenderloin, the softest and mildest, through New York Strip to Ribeye, the most marbled, and Porterhouse and T-Bone hold two of them on one bone. Brisket, Short Rib, Shank and Shoulder want hours of low heat, and braised Short Rib has no temperature to ask for. Pork Chop, Rack of Lamb and Duck Breast each say how the kitchen sends them. Salmon, Tuna, Swordfish and Halibut each carry a doneness note, Flounder, Snapper and Trout are the mild, lean fish, and Shrimp, Scallops, Oysters and Clams each carry a sizing or serving note.

The rest is the larder and the dessert menu, fastest by family: Parmesan, Ricotta, Feta and Blue Cheese; Grits, Risotto, Ravioli and Tortellini; Stock, Jus, Hollandaise, Vinaigrette and Pesto; Brioche, Sourdough, Puff Pastry and Tart. Sort the sweets by what holds them: Custard and Crème Brûlée by egg, Mousse by the whipped cream or whites folded in, Ice Cream, Sherbet and Sorbet by how much dairy is churned in. Then Jam against Compote by how far the fruit is cooked, Marmalade by its citrus peel, and Kimchi against a vinegar pickle, the sour grown rather than poured. Among the mushrooms, the pair is Truffle against Truffle Oil.

Save the nine menu words for last: Prix Fixe against Tasting Menu, À la Carte, Market Price, and the claims House-Made, Grass-Fed, Wild-Caught, Organic and Heirloom, each saying one narrow thing, not the wider thing a guest hears. Market Price has a job attached: know tonight's figure before service.

Take the doors in this order. Flip cards is where you read, one section at a time. Say it back is the one deck mode that counts as a round: recall before recognition. The written test is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers and no number: use it to find the section you skipped. The deck landing shows what is owed today. A card is met once it has been graded met or close in the deck's modes; a miss on its own is never met.
primers.next: Chef de Partie takes the deck to the station: Confit, Sous Vide, Rendered and Pan-Roasted as methods; Pancetta, Coppa, Pâté, Rillettes and Terrine on the board; Hanger, Skirt, Flank and Flat Iron steaks at the block; Branzino, Skate and Monkfish in the case; and the sauces beside them, Béarnaise, Béchamel, Demi-Glace and Aioli.

primers.lede: Folios for the first weeks: the chicken on your board, the spices in their whole form and the mushrooms in the walk-in, six subjects to each.
paragraphs: Each plate is a folio: one illustration keyed to six numbered subjects, a guide that names each one and says how to tell it from its neighbor, and a short list of sources for reading further. Commis holds Chicken: cuts and giblets, Spices: from fruit to flower and Mushrooms: six cultivated market forms. They are read, never graded, and nothing about them is recorded; the six questions at the foot of each folio are a quiet check for you alone.

Take the chicken first, because it is the bird you portion this week. Four subjects are the portions. The breast is the white meat of the chest; the thigh sits above the leg joint and the drumstick below it, both dark meat; and the wing carries the small drumette, which belongs to the wing and not the leg. The last two are the giblets a kitchen keeps. The liver is a soft organ, not a muscle cut, and the gizzard is the thick, muscular stomach that grinds the bird's food, which is how you tell the two apart.

Then the spices, each shown whole before it becomes a powder. Black pepper is the fruit of a tropical vine, and black, white and green peppercorns are one species handled three ways. Cumin is slender and ridged where coriander is round, and coriander is the seed of the plant whose leaves you call cilantro. Cinnamon is rolled bark, turmeric is an underground rhizome, and cloves are dried flower buds with no tie to a clove of garlic. The lesson of this folio is origin: know which part of the plant you are holding.

Leave the mushrooms for last. These are market mushrooms, not a guide for foraging. The white button, the cremini and the portobello are one species in three forms, so the color of the cap is not an age clock. Shiitake has an umbrella cap and a stem that can be tough enough to save for stock. Oyster mushrooms grow in fan-shaped clusters and take their name from their form, and maitake, also called hen of the woods, is a frilled cluster rather than a single cap.

Read the first plate opens the chicken folio, and The wall shows all twenty folios by kind, these three among them. Beneath each guide sits the original poster archive: the earlier poster, its transcription and the correction notes recorded against it, kept for reference. Learn from the six-subject guide, which is the current lesson, and open the archive only when you want the history.
primers.next: Chef de Partie hangs the folios for pork and beef, the Pacific, Atlantic and Gulf Coast fish cases, the vegetables and fruits of five regions, and cheese read through its milk, make and maturation.

primers.lede: Two faults open the repair table at Commis, flat and salty, and each has three levers you pull in order, one at a time.
paragraphs: The palate at Commis asks two things of you. Name flat and salty, the two faults the repair table opens with, each on a plate, and take each of the six tastes on the ladder to rung 1. These two faults come first because a commis meets them every shift: the soup that tastes of nothing and the stock reduced too far that sends the guest to the water glass. Between them they teach the one habit this subsection rests on. Taste, name the fault, pull one lever, taste again.

Flat is the fault where every flavor is present and none of it arrives, the dish tasting like a photograph of itself. Its levers run in a fixed order and the order is the lesson. Salt is always first, because most flat dishes are unsalted dishes. If the plate is already salted, acid is the next lever, not more salt. If it is salted and bright and still flat, umami is the third and the check ends there.

Salty is the fault that reaches for the water glass before the second bite. Its levers are dilute, bulk it out and counter it. Dilute means unsalted liquid or more of the base. Bulk it out means starch or cream, volume the salt has to spread through. Counter it means acid and a touch of sugar, which bend the perception without removing any salt. The potato trick mostly just dilutes, so count it as the dilute lever.

Take flat first. The table opens with it, and its first lever is the same one that causes salty when pulled too hard. Learn to salt in pinches with a taste between each, and you will reach for salty's levers far less often. Then take salty, and read its levers as an order as well: dilute and bulk before you counter.

The two doors do the work. The repair table lists the faults with their levers, in order, so open it with a plate in front of you and walk flat and salty lever by lever until the plate tells you which one it wanted. Calibrate is the tasting ladder, each taste to this level's rung, which at Commis is rung 1 for salt, sweet, acid, bitter, umami and seasoned. Salt, acid and umami are also the three levers of flat, so the ladder and the table teach each other.
Met here has one rule. A fault is met when it has been named on a plate in the repair table, and a taste when its ladder is cleared to this level's rung.
primers.next: Chef de Partie places sour and sweet on the palate, and asks the same of them: each named on a plate in the repair table, symptom first, then its levers in order.

primers.lede: Four things before you touch a station: the danger zone, the two-hour rule, cross-contamination and FIFO, read once and kept for good.
paragraphs: Food Safety at Commis is a short subsection and the one the whole kitchen assumes you already have. The items here fold into four ideas: the danger zone, the two-hour rule, cross-contamination and FIFO. The only thing asked of you is that you read it and carry it to the line.

Take the danger zone first, because the rest hangs off it. The guide states it as a band, 4 to 60 C (40 to 140 F), where pathogens multiply, and then states the one rule the band produces: the two-hour rule governs everything left in it. The same clause goes on to the cooling law, with its figures, its shallow pans and its ice baths, but the cooling law is placed at Chef de Partie, so read it now as the shape of what comes next. Notice what the guide states and what it leaves out: the band and the two hours are stated; what a cook does with a pan that has crossed the two hours is not, and this primer does not supply it.

Cross-contamination is the second idea, and the guide gives it three lines and nothing more: raw below ready-to-eat in storage, color-coded boards, and hands and towels as vectors. Read that as two controls and the vectors they answer, not as a full procedure. The guide names color-coded boards without stating which color belongs to which product, and this primer leaves that gap where the guide left it. What you can act on today is the order of the walk-in shelf and the towel on your shoulder: the first puts raw below ready-to-eat, the second the guide names as a vector.

FIFO comes last of the four because it is a habit rather than a fact: first in, first out, and the guide's practical gloss is to label and date everything, with its own aside that masking tape and a Sharpie run more restaurants than any software. The same clause names HACCP as the systematized version, identify hazards, control critical points, document, and names a service-critical and legal-critical protocol beside it. Both are placed at Chef de Partie, so at Commis you take the tape and the pen and leave the system for later. The room's half of that protocol is not deferred, though: Service on this page already asks it of you, in What We Screened and What We Did Not, as the one question you never answer from the app. The clause closes on the line worth keeping: none of this is glamour; all of it is the license to do the glamorous parts.

The doors are plain. Read: the Food Safety page at this level's first slice, and then the whole page, so you have seen where the cooling law and HACCP sit before anyone at the pass mentions them. Met here means you have read it; there is no exercise and nothing is written down about you.

primers.lede: Service at Commis is the words the room runs on, the screen you never answer from, the cut-off you can run and the bottle you can open and pour without ceremony.
paragraphs: Service at Commis runs in two pairs. The Room's Vocabulary and What We Screened and What We Did Not are about words: the ones the room runs on and the one question you never answer from the app. Responsible Service and the Law and The Bottle at the Table are about the drink in your hand: when to stop pouring, and the bottle you carry to the table.

Take The Room's Vocabulary first, because it is the first module and the first door opens on it. Its four terms are the pass and expediting, the brigade de cuisine, line slang, and service styles with front-of-house fluency. Its outcome is concrete: you act on "86 the halibut" without asking, you say "behind" without thinking, and you can name who is working the pass. The guide keeps menu format and service school as two separate axes, so state both for your room. Know what it does not teach: "dupe" is glossed in four words, and there is no fire or all-day sequencing anywhere, so reading a ticket is your room's lesson and not the track's.

What We Screened and What We Did Not is one term and one habit: you never answer a guest's question about what is in a dish from the app. The recipe screen is a text screen over the ingredient lines. It cannot see a shared fryer, a dusted board or a supplier's label, and a dish showing nothing means the screen found nothing, never that the dish is clear. The screen names what it checked and what it did not on every recipe, so the outcome is saying that in your own words to the guest who asks.

Responsible Service and the Law is one term from Cocktail & Bar, and its outcome is a cut-off you can run in order: slow the pace, water, food, then a clear kind no with a manager behind you. You check anyone who could plausibly be under 30, you know dram-shop liability makes the room civilly liable for a guest it overserved, and you can offer a good zero-proof or a spritz instead of a fourth negroni.

The Bottle at the Table has three terms: the sommelier's service ritual and floor fluency, wine faults, and decanting, temperature and glassware. The taste pour exists to check for faults and not preference. Corked smells of wet cardboard, oxidized of bruised apple, reduced of struck match, which may blow off if you wait. A corked bottle you replace graciously without arguing. Whites go out chilled, reds cool, just under room temperature. Present, open and pour without ceremony, and that is this module's outcome.

The doors on the level page are The first module, which opens The Room's Vocabulary; The track, all 27 modules; and the Drill, which runs the service drill over this level's modules with the whole track as the field. A module is met through its terms: every term of the module recalled met or close in the drill.

cites.name: What We Screened and What We Did Not

primers.lede: At this station a dish is a set of moves you repeat until they hold: the pan sauce, the braise, the dough and the fish.
paragraphs: Most plates here carry several techniques at once, and the braises and the bread ask you to hold a pot or a dough steady over hours. They run from the opening semesters of the Path of Study through the sauté station, the braise, bread and pastry fundamentals to Seafood Mastery, with one plate from the wok.

Start at the pan and the soup pot. Cacio e Pepe is toasted pepper, pecorino and the pasta's own starchy water brought into a sauce, and it tells you at once whether your salted water and your timing are right. Sole Meunière is the sauté station in one pan: dredge, sear, then brown butter. Bulgogi, from the wok semester, is the same hard sear on thin-cut meat that has been marinated first. Soupe à l'Oignon teaches the onion's patience, caramelizing slowly and deglazing before the broiler takes the top. Barszcz asks for a clear beet broth, strained and passed through a sieve.

Then the braise, where most of this level's hours go. Boeuf Bourguignon, Coq au Vin, Ragù alla Bolognese and Jamaican Oxtail Stew each build their base in the pan first, fat rendered or meat seared for color, before low heat and time do the rest. Take Bourguignon first because it sets the method. Coq au Vin adds reducing the sauce to finish, the ragù adds a fine dice for its base and a long, low simmer, and the oxtail adds skimming a long pot clear and taking sugar to caramel for the color of the gravy.

Then bread and pastry. Rosemary Focaccia is one technique, proofing, and the habit of reading the dough rather than the clock. Crème Brûlée is a custard tempered, strained and baked in a water bath, then finished with the torch. Crêpes look easy and are quick, but an even pan and a thin, even swirl take repetition before every one comes out the same.

Then the fish case. Cantonese Steamed Fish is steaming and a fine julienne. Miso-Glazed Black Cod is a marinade and the broiler. Linguine alle Vongole is clams steamed open and picked, their juices and the pasta water brought into an emulsion. Calamari Fritti is the coat, the deep fry and draining on a rack, never paper.

A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged: not read, not watched, cooked. The door "Read the semester" opens the Path at the semester that teaches the first dish you have not cooked; "Cook the next dish" goes straight to its recipe page; "The library at this level" shows the recipe grid at this level's difficulty when you want another plate. The Level test at the foot of the page asks across the subsections and ends on what you missed.
primers.next: At Sous Chef the plates move to live fire, the wok and longer builds: Jerk Chicken and the Whole Grilled Fish with Ladolemono over the coals, Char Kway Teow in the wok, the Country Sourdough Loaf and the Baguette de Tradition from the bread station, and Tarte au Citron and Profiteroles from pastry.

primers.lede: Chef de Partie technique is the station's work: the braise, the emulsion, the custard and the dough, done the same way every service.
paragraphs: The techniques placed here are what running a station asks, and most fall into four families: the sauce bench, the slow pot, the pastry and bread base, and the flavor builders. Béchamel sits on the sauce bench but is not an emulsion: it is milk thickened with a white roux. Confit, Rendering fat and The tagine share the braise's low, patient heat. Pie crust & blind baking and Icing & frosting open and close the pastry run.

Read Braising and Building an emulsion before the others, then cook them when the dishes list reaches the plates that carry them. Both carry written standards, and they teach two habits much of this level leans on: heat held below the boil, and nothing added faster than the pot can take it. A braise goes in deep brown, the liquid comes partway up and only trembles, a fork twists in with almost no resistance while the piece still lifts out whole, and the liquid ends as a sauce that coats a spoon. An emulsion thickens as the fat goes in, and fat never pools ahead of the work. When one breaks, whisking harder does nothing: start a fresh base and work the broken sauce into it slowly. Hollandaise and Beurre blanc are that same rule on the sauce station.

Then the pastry and bread base, each read by its own mark. Rubbing fat into flour stops early, while pieces of cold fat still show. Creaming butter & sugar takes minutes, not seconds, until the mix is pale and grown in volume. Folding stops the moment the streaks go. Kneading dough ends smooth and barely tacky, Resting dough lets it roll without springing back, and Proofing is judged on volume and the poke test, never by the hour. Tempering a custard and The water bath share one discipline: gentle heat, no boil, and doneness judged by how it behaves. Sugar stages & caramel adds the last: nothing stirred once it boils, every stage read by temperature or test.

Tadka and Pounding a curry paste are about order: the hardest seeds into hot fat first and the delicate ones last, the hard dry ingredients pounded down before anything wet arrives. Fermentation is a rate, not a duration, so taste it rather than trust the hours. Marinating is the one technique where longer is a different result, not a safer one: keep the stated time and keep it cold. Pleating dumplings and Working with masa carry standards of their own: a seam closed its whole length, masa that seals smooth when a pinch is rolled shut. Pierogi, Handling phyllo and Fresh pasta are other kitchens' dough work, and Risotto method, Congee, Shucking shellfish and The seafood boil are narrower methods, each learned on its own recipes.

A technique with a written standard is met when you cook one of its recipes and are graded met against that standard; one without a standard is met by cooking any of its recipes. The Read the techniques door opens the index at this level. The next technique door takes you to the first one you have not met. The Level test at the foot of the page runs across the subsections and ends on what you missed, with the right answers.

primers.lede: At this station a word is a method: the sear, the emulsion, the cut, the fish case, the baker's math and the spice rack, each owed a sentence when the menu names it.
paragraphs: Start with the words your station cooks by. Take The Maillard Reaction first: browning between amino acids and sugars, whose enemies are water and crowding, and a different thing from caramelization, which is sugar alone. Once you can say why a wet steak steams, the sear in Braising & Stewing explains itself. Then Emulsions: fat and water held together as droplets by an emulsifier such as egg yolk or mustard, the physics behind mayonnaise, hollandaise, vinaigrette and beurre blanc, and the same trick as the starchy pasta water that turns oil and butter into a clinging sauce. Confit and Consommé & Clarification finish the group: fat as a gentle cooking medium, and a raft of egg white, ground meat and mirepoix that filters a stock clear.

The cuts and the fish case come next, because a guest asks about them by name. Read Marbling first: the grades are largely measures of it, and more of it forgives a higher doneness. Flank, Skirt & Hanger share one law: marinate or salt, high heat to medium-rare at most, rest, and slice thin against the grain. Dry-Aging buys flavor through moisture loss and the meat's own enzymes. At the fish case, Round Fish vs. Flat Fish tells you two fillets or four, Fatty vs. Lean Fish tells you smoke or a gentle poach, and Smoked Fish, hot or cold, names two products sharing one word.

Pastry and baking science sit here at their base. Take Gluten & Hydration first: hydration is water measured against the flour's weight, and baker's math, everything written relative to the flour, is the language every formula scales in. Chemical Leaveners follows: baking soda needs an acid partner and also speeds browning, while baking powder carries its own acid. Caramel Stages & Sugar Work closes the group: the syrup's temperature decides what it becomes, from thread and soft ball through crack to true caramel, and a wet caramel is more forgiving while a dry one is faster and riskier, with crystallization as the saboteur.

Then the spice rack and the less common produce. Building the Working Spice Pantry names the core dozen, and Toasting, Blooming & the Tadka Doctrine explains why the pan matters: most spice flavor dissolves in fat, not water, which is why raw curry powder tastes dusty and chili crisp works. Acid Architecture and Sweetness as Seasoning are the palate's sour and sweet in words; read them side by side. Open the produce with Chile Fluency (Fresh & Dried), because in Mexican kitchens a dried chile takes a new name: the ripe red poblano, dried, is Ancho. Then read the Seasonal Larder entries, Citrus in Winter among them, by what your menu handles this month, framed by Seasonality & Ripeness.

The first door, Read the terms, is the Lexicon at this level: take one group at a sitting and say each word aloud as the sentence a server would need. Then Flashcards and Quiz, both over this level's terms. A term is met when you have recalled it met or close on the flashcard ladder or in the quiz; a miss alone is never met.
primers.next: At Sous Chef the Lexicon moves to the pass and the office: Lamination at the pastry bench, Wok Hei & Stir-Fry Discipline and Grilling vs. Barbecue vs. Smoking on the line, Menu Economics and Prime Cost behind it, and rarer produce such as Black Truffle and Buddha's Hand.

primers.lede: At Chef de Partie the deck is the menu's second layer: the words a guest points at and expects a sentence back, from confit to 'nduja to pot de crème.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie hands you the cards the floor asks about: what the thing is, how the kitchen handles it and what it is not. Most carry a note or a not-this line, and that is where the misses happen: coppa is not prosciutto, ghee is not clarified butter, a macaron is not a macaroon. Wherever a card has a pair, learn the pair.

Take the six methods first, they describe everything else: confit, sous vide, blanched, fermented, rendered and pan-roasted. Confit and rendered pull opposite ways, meat under fat against fat out of meat. Then the sauces, the mother sauces the level page names first, and their children: béchamel is the white base, demi-glace the roasted veal stock reduced by half and the base of bordelaise, béarnaise a child of hollandaise, and emulsion explains why aioli and remoulade hold. The cold, sharp ones travel together, mignonette, chimichurri and salsa verde; coulis is the sweet strained purée under dessert.

Cuts come in two kinds of card: the steaks, hanger steak, skirt steak, flank steak, flat iron steak and ribeye cap, plus wagyu, a breed and not a cut, most giving the doneness the kitchen sends, and the braises, cheek and oxtail, with no temperature to ask for. Meats are the lean, farm-raised ones to explain, guinea hen against pheasant, quail, rabbit, venison, and the plates that need an honest word, foie gras, chicken liver, bone marrow, beef tongue. Charcuterie learns in contrasts: pancetta against bacon, coppa against prosciutto, pâté against terrine against rillettes, soppressata against 'nduja. The fish case is branzino against black sea bass, skate, monkfish, arctic char, blue crab and soft-shell crab, roe against caviar.

Dairy is a ladder of clarified butter, brown butter and ghee, then compound butter, chèvre, burrata, mascarpone and crème fraîche. Starches split into shapes and grains, tagliatelle against pappardelle, cavatelli against orecchiette, agnolotti and gnocchi, then farro, bulgur, polenta and arborio. Mushrooms are foraged, chanterelle, morel, porcini, or farmed, king trumpet, hen of the woods, and the notes on morel and enoki say cooked through. The preparations split the raw plate, carpaccio against tartare, ceviche, tataki and gravlax, from the cooked one: ragout, croquette, roulade, amandine.

Pastry runs from beignets, galette, pavlova and soufflé to the custards, crème anglaise against pastry cream, panna cotta and pot de crème, and the frozen four, gelato, granita, parfait and semifreddo. The pantry is the seasoning rack: miso, fish sauce, harissa, pimentón, sherry vinegar, preserved lemon, finishing salt. Language holds the menu's claims, dry-aged, pasture-raised, heritage breed and day-boat, and the not-this line says what each word is not.

Flip cards first, the whole card, note and not-this included. Say it back is the one deck mode that counts as a round, recall before recognition, so give it the most time. The written test is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers and no number, so take it after a run of Say it back. The deck's landing shows what is owed today. A card is met when it has been graded met or close in the deck's modes; a miss alone is never met, so take a missed card through Say it back again.
primers.next: Sous Chef adds the specialist word on these shelves: squab, sweetbreads and poussin; guanciale, lardo, speck, tasso, bresaola and jamón ibérico on the board; bavette and coulotte; turbot, sturgeon, tilefish, wreckfish and cobia; velouté, gastrique and romesco; crudo, escabeche and clafoutis; the floor cards for beurre blanc and pâte à choux, which the Chef de Partie techniques already teach; and garde manger itself.

primers.lede: The folios for running a station: the two big animals, the three fish cases, the vegetables and fruits of five regions, and the cheese board.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie holds most of the wall. Each folio teaches six subjects with a guide, a line to remember for each and sources to read further; they are read, never graded, and nothing about them is recorded. Read them in four groups, in the order a station meets them: the meat, the fish, the produce and the cheese.

Start with Pork: six useful distinctions and Beef: where the cut begins, because a station orders by cut. The pork folio runs from the Boston butt of the shoulder through the loin and the tenderloin to the fresh belly, the spare ribs and the hock. The beef folio places the chuck roast, the ribeye, the strip steak, the tenderloin, the brisket and the hanger steak on the animal, and its lines to remember are the ones a server gets wrong: marbling is fat within the muscle, the strip loin and the tenderloin are neighboring but separate muscles, and the hanger is not the flank.

Then the three fish cases. Pacific: six seafood identities asks you to read body shape and fins before a market nickname: king is another name for Chinook, and the fish sold as black cod is sablefish, not a cod. Atlantic: fish and shellfish sets four finfish beside the sea scallop and the American lobster, and Gulf Coast: reef, open water and shore runs from red snapper and grouper to mahi mahi, yellowfin tuna, white shrimp and blue crab.

The ten produce folios read in pairs by region: Northwest vegetables and Northwest fruits, Southwest vegetables and Southwest fruits, Midwest vegetables and Midwest fruits, Northeast vegetables and Northeast fruits, Southeast vegetables and Southeast fruits. Each teaches the part of the plant you are holding, the shoot, root, bud, pod, leaf or fruit, rather than a season, because availability moves with the grower and the weather. Take your own region first and read the rest as the menu brings them in.

Finish with Cheese: milk, make and maturation, which reads a cheese through its milk, texture and method before its color: the crystals in Parmigiano Reggiano are not mold, and an orange Cheddar is not an older one for its color alone. Read the first plate opens the first folio at this level, and The wall shows all twenty. Each folio keeps the original poster archive beneath its guide, with the correction notes recorded against the poster; the guide is the lesson.

primers.lede: Sour and sweet are the Chef de Partie faults: the ones a station's own reductions and pan sauces make when the ratio slips, and each one is a lever against the other.
paragraphs: Commis opened the repair table on flat and salty, the faults on either side of the salt cellar. Chef de Partie moves to sour and sweet. What they share: unlike flat, neither is fixed by adding what is missing. Both are faults of excess, like salty, and excess does not pour back out of a pot. The work at this level is learning what stands against each, in what order, and what each lever costs.

Take sour first, the order the repair table keeps. Its symptom is exact: the acid arrives first and is still there after everything else has gone. Fat buffers rather than removes, so butter mounted in or a spoon of cream softens the edge without touching the acid itself. Sweetness is the other buffer, held below the threshold of tasting sweet: you are covering a fault, not making a sweet sauce. Baking soda neutralizes chemically, but pinches only, because it eats brightness along with the fault. Time mellows on its own, if you have any. Read that list as a lesson in restraint: two levers hide the fault, one changes the pot at a cost, and the last is time, which a service never has.

Then sweet. The symptom is cloying by the third mouthful, with nothing to cut through it. Acid cuts. Salt reframes: the same sugar reads as seasoning rather than dessert. Bitterness opposes it directly, and the table names the sources: coffee, cocoa, char. Heat, the chile kind, distracts from it. Side by side the pair is a mirror: sweetness is the second lever for sour, acid is the first lever for sweet. A fault is a taste that leads and stays; the fix is a measured dose of its lever, tasted after every addition.

The subsection opens two doors. The repair table holds the faults with their levers, in order: read sour and sweet there lever by lever, then find a real sauce that shows the symptom and name the fault before you reach for anything. Calibrate is the tasting ladder, and at Chef de Partie it asks every taste, salt, sweet, acid, bitter, umami and seasoned, to rung 2. The ladder climbs all six, not only the faults placed here: it trains the tongue that will catch them.

Met here means two things: a fault is met when it has been named on a plate in the repair table, and a taste when its ladder is cleared to this level's rung. For this subsection that is sour and sweet each named on a plate, and the six tastes brought to rung 2 on Calibrate. Do the repair table first, because you cannot name what you have not read, and take Calibrate in short sittings between services, since the palate tires.
primers.next: Sous Chef asks the same of bitter and rich, the faults placed there, and takes the tasting ladder to its next rung.

primers.lede: Food safety at Chef de Partie is the cooling law and the way you actually cool, HACCP as a system, and the allergen protocol, which the guide calls critical twice.
paragraphs: Commis gave you the danger zone and the two-hour rule. Chef de Partie asks you to own what happens to the stockpot after service, because a station makes more hot food than one service eats. The entries here sit in two pairs. The cooling law and the cooling method are one practice, stated as a number and as a technique. HACCP and the last entry are two systems a station runs inside. Take the cooling pair first.

The cooling law is the guide's own figure: hot food to 21 C (70 F) within 2 hours, then to 4 C (39 F) within 4 more. The guide gives the two windows and nothing more; how your code counts them is the code's to say. How you get there is the cooling method: shallow pans, ice baths, never a stockpot straight into the walk-in. A full pot holds its heat for hours in a cold room and warms everything shelved around it, the slow cooling the two-hour rule at Commis already governs. Ladle the stock into shallow pans, or stand the pot in an ice bath and stir, and the law becomes something a station can meet.

HACCP is the systematized version of what Commis taught as habit: identify hazards, control critical points, document. Those three verbs are the whole of the entry at Chef de Partie. So read HACCP here as a way of seeing your station, the moments where a time or a temperature decides whether the food is right and the log that proves you watched them. The figures come from your code and your chef, not from the guide.

The last entry is the shortest and the heaviest: the allergen protocol, which the guide calls service-critical and legal-critical. The guide says so twice, and that is the whole of the Chef de Partie entry. What you can act on at Chef de Partie is knowing where your house keeps its protocol, following it as your house set it, and never improvising one.

Nothing here is met or missed: food safety is read, never graded, and nothing about it is recorded. The level page opens two doors. The first is Read: the Food Safety page at this level's first slice. The second is The whole page. Take the first slice first, this level's entries, then read the whole page once for the gaps, what the guide names without stating.

primers.next: Sous Chef asks you to run the kitchen so any moment is inspection-ready: temps logged, FIFO labeled, hand sinks stocked and used, sanitizer buckets titrated. It asks what you do during a visit and after one, and with an illness complaint: take it seriously and kindly, gather specifics, preserve records and product, and remember that the cover-up is always worse than the event.

primers.lede: Service at Chef de Partie is the glass explained: how a wine is described, the two pairing games, the bottles you will pour, and the cheese board's formula.
paragraphs: Commis gave you the room's vocabulary and the bottle at the table. Chef de Partie asks you to say what is in the glass and put it next to a plate on purpose. The modules here fall into four groups: the grammar of wine, the cellar you will pour from, everything that is not wine, and the cheese board.

Take How a Wine Is Described first, because every module after it uses its seven terms: acidity, tannin, body, dry and off-dry, oak, terroir, vintage. You have it when you answer "is it dry?" and "is it heavy?" correctly, know that off-dry is not sweet, and can hear which lever a guest means by "something smooth". Then The Two Games and the Switches. Every pairing is congruent, echoing the dish, or contrast, opposing it, and one switch does the work: salt loves acid and bubbles, fat wants cutting acid or matching richness, food acid demands equal wine acid, chile is inflamed by alcohol and tannin, sweet dishes need sweeter wine, bitter stacks with tannin, umami makes tannin harsh. Name the game and the switch in one sentence: that is what you say at the table.

The cellar comes next, whites before reds. The Whites You Will Pour leads with three grapes, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling, three sentences each, with the aromatic whites beside Sauvignon Blanc. Two facts matter most: Riesling is the answer to chile heat, and Chardonnay's oak level must match the butter level. The Reds You Will Pour runs from the Bordeaux blend and Pinot Noir through the Rhône school and the food-wine trinity to the New World crowd-pleasers; its test is steering a table off Cabernet when the plate is chile or delicate fish. Bubbles, Sherry and the Fortified End sells Champagne as the rescue for almost any plate, not a toast, tells Prosecco from Cava from Pét-Nat, sets Fino beside Manzanilla, and matches Port or Madeira to cheese or chocolate.

Everything That Is Not Wine covers the rest of the list. Beer pairs by its two families, sake climbs a polishing ladder and has a right serving temperature, tea and coffee are a service and not an afterthought, and a guest who is not drinking deserves a genuine non-alcoholic pairing. Take it straight after the cellar, while the pairing games are still fresh.

The cheese board closes the service track at Chef de Partie, and its spine is a formula. The Board: Formula and Families asks for 3 to 5 cheeses spanning milk, texture and volume, 30 to 50 g a head, always at room temperature an hour out, and asks you to place any cheese in one of five families: fresh, bloomy, washed, semi-hard to hard, or blue. It also says why halloumi holds its shape under heat and gruyère flows. The Levant, South Asia and the Americas then covers the cheeses outside the classical board: paneer, akkawi and nabulsi, labneh, the Mexican trio and the American four, including why American cheese is engineered the way it is. Serve them without apology or condescension.

Now the doors. Open the first module and work down the list in this order. The track shows all 27 modules and where this level's modules sit. The drill runs over this level's modules with the whole track as the field, and it is where met is decided: a module is met through its terms, every term of the module recalled met or close in the drill.

primers.next: Sous Chef takes the same subject wider: The Grape Atlas as deep reference, the cheese boards by country (The Italian Board, The French Board, Alpine and Iberian, Britain, the Low Countries and the Cold Edge), the charcuterie boards from The Italian Salumi to The Spanish Cure, How It Was Cured as reference, and What Is in the Bottle.

primers.lede: At Sous Chef a dish is a whole station in miniature: live fire, the wok, a long ferment or a build in parts, cooked and logged, then cooked again until you could teach it.
paragraphs: These plates are fire and smoke, the wok, seafood, and the Advanced plates with a long wait or a build in parts. The long waits are the Birria de Res con Consomé, which runs from a marinade to a sear to a braise to the griddle, and the breads: the Pizza Margherita, the Baguette de Tradition and the Country Sourdough Loaf live on fermentation and proofing. The builds in parts are pastry: the Tarte au Citron asks for a blind-baked crust, a lemon cream over a water bath and, if you crown it, a meringue, while the Profiteroles (Pâte à Choux Master) take one pastry technique to a finish.

Take them in the order of the Path of Study, which is the order the doors follow, and start with the birria. It rewards the braise you already know from Chef de Partie and runs well over four hours, so give it an open afternoon. That week, feed a sourdough starter into life as preparation: the Country Sourdough Loaf leans on one, and a new starter needs time before it can raise a loaf. Then take the breads: the Pizza Margherita first, then the Baguette de Tradition, where proofing and steam decide the crust, then the loaf.

In pastry, take the Profiteroles before the tart. Choux is one technique carried to a finish, and one is easier to log honestly than three. The Tarte au Citron stacks the crust, the cream and the meringue, and each part can fail on its own.

The fire plates teach the coals. Take Huli Huli Chicken first: butchery basics before the fire, then the turn, since huli means turn and the sugar in the baste burns if the chicken sits. Jerk Chicken comes next, once the two-zone fire is second nature, because jerk brings a technique of its own to the coals. Memphis Dry-Rub Ribs follow, and low and slow smoking is hours of holding the fire steady on thin blue smoke.

The wok plates are the fastest cooking in the guide and the least forgiving: maximum heat, total mise and small batches leave no second look. Cook the Rau Muong Xao Toi first and often, until the garlic turns fragrant and the greens follow before it scorches, then the Pad Krapow Moo, where the pork is pressed into the wok to sear, not stew, then Char Kway Teow, the Advanced plate of the three. The Whole Grilled Fish with Ladolemono comes last and brings back the coals: a whole fish over the fire, filleting, and the oil and lemon emulsion that dresses it.

A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged. Read the semester opens the Path of Study at the semester teaching the first dish you have not cooked, and Cook the next dish goes straight to that recipe; both keep the order above, so they open on the birria until it is logged. The library at this level is the recipe grid filtered to Advanced, which leaves out the fire plates, the fish and the two quicker wok plates placed here. Log each plate the day you cook it, then cook it again until you could talk a commis through it at the pass. The Level test at the foot of the page ends on what you missed, with the right answers.
primers.next: At Chef the dishes become projects: the capstone semester and the Advanced library's project dishes, from Central Texas Smoked Brisket and Tacos al Pastor (Home Trompo) to Sauce Espagnole & Demi-Glace, Salt-Baked Whole Fish and Baked Alaska.

primers.lede: At Sous Chef a technique is read from the pass: the fire, the wok, the fold and the knife.
paragraphs: A grill run on flames, a crowded wok or butter that shatters in the fold shows on the plate, so a sous has to know each of these well enough to see the fault from across the kitchen and teach the fix. Take Grilling over live coals first. It carries a written standard, sits under more recipes than anything else here, and its marks teach the fire before the food: coals evenly under gray ash with no flames licking through, a hot zone and a cooler one both ready, a hot clean grate the food releases from, marks browned rather than burnt, and an interior at its target with a thin gradient. Low & slow smoking comes next, with its own standard: thin blue smoke, never white and rolling, a chamber held steady with the air intake, the stall waited out or wrapped through on purpose, and doneness read by probe and feel, never by the clock.

Asado fire and Jerk carry no written standard, and they are not the same fire. For asado, wood burns down in a separate fire and its embers are raked under the grill as the cook needs them. Jerk cooks over pimento wood, often covered, so it grills and smokes at once. Take them once the two-zone fire is second nature.

Wok technique carries the third standard. Everything goes in dry and in order, the wok stays loud from first moment to last, every piece is glossy with no sauce pooled under it, and the vegetables keep their color and a bite at the center. Its fault is nearly always too much at once or too wet. Take Velveting alongside it: meat coated in egg white and cornstarch, rested and precooked briefly, which is where stir-fry silk comes from.

Lamination, Letter-folding dough and Tempering chocolate are temperature disciplines with no written standard, so the recipe is the teacher. In lamination the dough and the butter must match, cold but bendable; the dough rests between folds, and the turns are counted, a letter fold being one single turn. Butter too cold shatters and leaks; too warm, it smears in and bakes like brioche. Tempering chocolate is melting, cooling and reheating along a set curve so the cocoa butter sets in its stable form: gloss and snap instead of dull bloom.

Butchery basics and Filleting fish are where cooking starts before there is heat: frenching a rack, butterflying to an even thickness, tying a roast for even cooking and clean slices, stripping silverskin, and drawing a flexible fillet knife along the spine. A sous reads the yield in the trim bin, and yield follows the edge.

A technique with a written standard is met when you cook one of its recipes and are graded met against its marks. For the rest, cooking any one of its recipes meets it. Open Read the techniques for the index at this level, and The next technique takes you to the first one not yet met.
primers.next: At Chef the techniques are the ones nobody drills by accident, on the fewest recipes and taught by no semester: Mole, Biryani & dum, Hand-pulled noodles, Paella & socarrat, Tandoor breads and The soufflé among them.

primers.lede: At the pass the words turn specialist and the numbers arrive: the fire, the fold, what a plate really costs and the rare thing a guest asks you to explain.
paragraphs: This is the vocabulary you teach from as well as cook from, and it runs in bands: the fire and the fold whose standard a whole service answers to, the numbers that run the building, then the spices and the specialist produce a guest asks about because it is on tonight's board. Take them in that order.

Start with the fire and the fold. Grilling vs. Barbecue vs. Smoking separates three fires by their timing: grilling is direct high heat for minutes over a two-zone grate, barbecue is indirect low heat and wood smoke for hours on collagen cuts, and smoking either cooks as it flavors or, cold, flavors cured food without cooking it. Keep the two wok words apart: Wok Hei & Stir-Fry Discipline names the aroma, the smoky, singed-air breath of food and oil vaporizing against hot carbon steel, and The Wok names the vessel, whose sloped walls give a searing base and cooler shoulders to stage ingredients. Lamination is the layered dough itself, butter and dough folded into alternating sheets that oven steam jacks apart. The method behind all three belongs to the Techniques reader.

Then the numbers, and Menu Economics: Food Cost, Yield & Par first, because the rest lean on it. Cost a fish at its raw invoice price instead of its price after trim and cooking, and the plate costs more than you think. Prime Cost adds total labor to cost of goods and wants it weekly, not only at month-end. COGS Control sets actual against theoretical cost and reads the variance as the leak; Labor schedules to forecast, not habit; KPIs & the Daily Dashboard keeps few numbers on one page. Health Inspections & Crisis Management is the entry the Food Safety page reads clause by clause at this level, so read it there.

The spice entries teach a behavior more than a taste. Asafoetida (Hing) goes into hot fat first, a pinch, and blooms into savory allium depth; Panch Phoron keeps its seeds whole and uses their crackle as the timer; The Three Heats sorts chile, pepper and mustard heat into linger, hum and flash. The larder is learned by the menu, the dish on the board first: Seville Orange for marmalade and bigarade, Treviso grilled as precoce or raw as tardivo, Black Truffle carried in fat, Nettles blanched on arrival in gloves, Salsify peeled into lemon water, Lovage counted in leaves.

Open Read the terms, then Flashcards and Quiz over this level's terms. A term is met when you have recalled it met or close on the flashcard ladder, or in the quiz; a miss alone is never met. Then check yourself: can you explain yield to a new cook, or tardivo to a guest, without the card?

primers.next: At Chef the numbers become the whole building: the business plan, the lease, the pro forma, the P&L line by line, break-even and cash flow. The larder goes rarer too, to Matsutake, Mangosteen, Cardoon and Puntarelle, words a senior cook owns without notes.

primers.lede: At Sous Chef the deck is the classical menu word and the specialist product behind it, known well enough to teach.
paragraphs: These cards are the words a fine-dining menu prints without a gloss and expects the floor to carry. Most fall into three families. First, the classical methods, sauces and preparations: À la Plancha, Salt-Baked and Lacquered; Beurre Blanc, Velouté, Bordelaise, Gribiche and Soubise; Meunière, En Papillote, En Croûte, Torchon and Quenelle. Second, specialist product: the cuts, Bavette, Coulotte, Denver Steak, Teres Major and Chateaubriand; the cured meats from Guanciale and Lardo to Speck, Bresaola and Jamón Ibérico; the fish case of Turbot, Dover Sole, Langoustine and Uni; the wild Black Trumpet and White Truffle, and the Summer Truffle, which is also farmed. Third, the pastry section's words, from Pâte à Choux and Canelé to Sabayon, Crémeux and Posset.

Take the pairs first, because at this level the question is less what a word means than what it is not. Gastrique and Agrodolce are both sugar and vinegar, one a smooth syrup built on caramel, the other often chunky with fruit and onion. Crudo and Escabeche are both set against ceviche: one raw and dressed at the last moment, the other always cooked before it meets the vinegar. En Papillote is a paper parcel torn open; En Croûte is a pastry wrapper you eat. Meunière is browned butter and lemon, where Beurre Blanc is pale butter whisked into a wine reduction. Learn them in twos.

Then the product, read with its note, because this is where a guest's question comes back to the pass. Bavette and Denver Steak are best at medium rare and sliced across the grain. Chateaubriand is one roast, so both guests share one doneness. Squab breast is classically medium rare, so ask before it fires. Dover Sole is filleted from the bone at the table, so a stray fine bone is possible. Tell Speck from prosciutto, Tasso from andouille and Stracciatella from burrata the way the cards do.

Take the pastry and the room's language next, and do not skip their warnings. A pale Canelé is the failure, not a dark one. Kouign-Amann folds its sugar inside a yeasted dough. Clafoutis may keep its cherry pits, so ask the kitchen. Garde Manger is the cold station, and its crudo and oysters go out raw. Mignardises close the meal where an amuse-bouche opens it. Omakase prints no menu, so anything a guest needs to avoid is said before the first course, and Regenerative has no legal definition, so the farm's name is what counts.

Start at the deck landing, which shows what is owed today, then Flip cards at this level, then Say it back, recall before recognition and the one deck mode that counts as a round. A card is met when it has been graded met or close in the deck's modes; a miss alone is never met. The written test for this level is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers and no number, so treat its misses as tomorrow's flips.
primers.next: At Chef the deck narrows to the rare, the specialist and the deeply classical word a senior cook or server must own without notes: Ballotine and Grenobloise, Moulard and Secreto Ibérico, Washed Rind, Bottarga, Ikejime and Koji-Aged.

primers.lede: One folio at Sous Chef: the charcuterie board by cut and by process, six products a sous must explain without notes.
paragraphs: Sous Chef holds a single folio, Charcuterie: cut and process. Like every folio it teaches six subjects with a guide and sources, and it is read, never graded; nothing about it is recorded. It sits here because a board is judged by the difference between its products, and a sous is the one asked to explain that difference to a guest and to a new cook.

Read it by cut first. Prosciutto di Parma is a dry-cured whole-muscle ham from the rear leg of the pig. Pancetta is cured belly and guanciale is cured cheek or jowl, so the two are different cuts even when both are used for their fat. Bresaola della Valtellina is the beef on the board, a cured whole muscle from the hindquarter, and it is the reminder that not everything on a board is pork.

Then read it by process. Salame Milano is a cured sausage whose fat sits in fine flecks the size of rice grains; Mortadella Bologna is a cooked, finely ground pork sausage set with larger white cubes of fat. That pair carries the folio's main point: charcuterie takes in cooked products as well as dry-cured ones. The guide is a map of product identities, not a curing method, and the specification of the product you serve belongs to its producer, so ask the kitchen which ones the house buys.

Read the first plate opens this folio, and The wall shows all twenty, the folios read at Commis and Chef de Partie among them; read those again when the menu calls for them. The folio is the picture, not the drill: every subject on it but guanciale is a term in The Italian Salumi, the Service module at this level, and that drill is where they are met. Beneath the guide sits the original poster archive with its recorded correction notes, kept for reference, while the six-subject guide is the lesson.
primers.next: Chef holds no folio of its own. At that level the wall is read again with the menu in hand, and the folios become the way you teach the brigade the distinctions learned here.

primers.lede: Bitter and rich are the two faults placed here, and neither reads in a moment: one stays after the swallow, the other only shows by the sixth bite.
paragraphs: The repair table opened at Commis on flat and salty, and Chef de Partie added sour and sweet. Those four faults are read in the moment of tasting. The two placed here ask for more time. Bitter is a hard edge at the back of the palate that stays after swallowing, so you judge it after the spoon is down, not only during. Rich is delicious for two bites and fatiguing by the sixth, so a single taste says the plate is good. That is why these two sit at the sous chef's level: the sous is the one who tastes a portion through, not a spoon.

Take Bitter first, because it has four levers and asks you to choose between them. Salt comes first: it suppresses bitterness outright, real chemistry and not folklore. Sweetness buffers it. Fat rounds it off. Acid brightens past it rather than removing it. Three of the four soften the edge itself; only acid leaves it in place and brightens past it. So when a charred dish or a bitter green comes up hard, salt before you reach for honey, butter or lemon, and taste again after each move. One lever at a time, or you cannot tell which one worked.

Rich is the simpler fault with the stricter answer. The lever is acid, always acid, and there is no second answer to this one. After the acid, and not instead of it, comes something crunchy-fresh. A crunchy garnish on its own gives the guest one bite of contrast and then the fatigue returns; the acid is what resets the palate so the sixth bite tastes like the first. When a braise, a cream sauce or a fatty cut comes up heavy, adjust with acid, taste past the second bite, and only then add the crunch.

The two faults teach each other. Salt, whose excess you named as salty at Commis, is now the first lever for bitter. Acid, which you named as sour at Chef de Partie, is now the only answer to rich. The chemistry is not new at this level; reading a plate over time instead of in a moment is. Spend your first sessions on plates that hold up on one taste and fail on six, or that leave an edge after the swallow, and say which fault it is before you pick the lever.

Two doors open from this subsection. The repair table holds the faults with their levers, in order, and a fault is met when you have named it on a plate there. Calibrate holds the tasting ladder, which at this level asks each of the six tastes, salt, sweet, acid, bitter, umami and seasoned, to rung 3, and a taste is met when its ladder is cleared to this rung. Bitter is on both doors, as a fault to repair and as a taste to calibrate; rich is a fault only, and the ladder does not carry it.
primers.next: Chef takes the palate to spicy and muddy, the faults with the least obvious levers. The slow reading you built here, to the sixth bite and not the first, is what you carry up.

primers.lede: At Sous Chef the inspector is not an event to prepare for: the kitchen you run every day is the one that gets photographed.
paragraphs: Commis gave you the danger zone and FIFO, Chef de Partie the cooling law and HACCP as a system. Sous Chef moves the subject from your station to the whole room, because a sous is the one standing there when the inspector walks in and the one who writes up what happens after. Placed here are the Inspections clause, The principle beneath it, the facts drawn from them, and one gap. Read the Inspections clause first and in full, because every fact at this level is a line lifted out of it.

The first group is the standard itself. The guide says to run the kitchen so ANY moment is inspection-ready, and its capitals are the point: there is no prep week. The daily standard it names is temps logged, FIFO labeled, hand sinks stocked and USED, sanitizer buckets titrated, and USED carries as much weight as ANY, since a stocked sink nobody touches is a finding waiting to be written. Take this group before the other two, because it is the part you can walk the line and check tonight.

The second group is the visit. During it, accompany professionally, correct on the spot what can be, never argue, get every finding in writing. After it, fix, document, retrain at pre-shift, and treat repeat findings as management failures, not staff ones. That last phrase is the sous chef's line in the whole subsection: a finding that comes back is yours, not the commis's. Read these two facts together and in that order, because the second only works if the first left you with paper.

The third group is one of the crisis playbooks, written before it is needed. On a foodborne-illness complaint, take it seriously and kindly, gather specifics, preserve records and product. Then call the insurer and, if credible, the health department yourself, because the cover-up is always worse than the event. The principle beneath the Inspections clause says why: crises are inevitable, scandals are optional, and the difference is preparation, documentation, and guests first, reputation second, ego never. Read the principle twice.

One gap is placed here on purpose. Sanitizer buckets titrated is a discipline the guide names, but to what concentration it never says. The app does not fill that in, and neither does this page. Knowing which lines the guide states and which it only names is itself a Sous Chef skill, and the level above makes a subject of it.

There are two doors. Read opens the Food Safety page at this level's first slice, and The whole page opens all of it, worth doing once here so the playbook sits on the Commis and Chef de Partie material. Met is simple: food safety is read, never graded, and nothing about it is recorded.

primers.lede: Service at Sous Chef is the board and the list: the grapes behind the glass, the cheeses and cured meats by country, and what is in the well and call bottles behind the bar.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie gave you how a wine is described and the board's formula. Sous Chef asks you to sell off the list and the board from depth. The modules here fall in four groups: one grape atlas, four cheese boards, six charcuterie modules and one bar shelf. Take them in that order unless you work the bar, where the bottle comes second.

Take The Grape Atlas (Deep Reference) first, because the floor uses it every night. Seventeen varietals, Riesling to Zinfandel, and for each you can say where it comes from, what it smells like and what it does at the table. Work the grapes in pairs, Chardonnay against Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir against Gamay, so each has a neighbor.

The cheese boards come next, in the order the page lists them. The Italian Board and The French Board come first and carry the most cheeses: why the crunch in aged Parmigiano is a feature, Gorgonzola dolce against piccante, why Époisses smells worse than it tastes, and how to stop a guest cutting the nose off a wedge of Comté. Alpine and Iberian sells the melting cheeses on their physics and places Cabrales as the blue that outguns Roquefort. Britain, the Low Countries and the Cold Edge closes the boards with Stilton, aged Gouda, and the four that behave unlike any of them: feta, halloumi, brunost, sulguni.

Charcuterie is the largest group and it has an order. Start with The Charcuterie Board, the two churches of whole muscle and fermented salami on one slicer, because its outcome is the standard you hold the pass to: 3 to 5 meats spanning silk, salame, spreadable and a wildcard, 60 to 90 g a head, whole-muscle sliced translucent and salame in 2 to 3 mm coins on a slight bias, everything at room temperature 20 to 30 minutes out and cut as close to service as possible.

After that the modules go by region. The Italian Salumi tells Parma from San Daniele and coppa from culatello. The Spanish Cure gives you the bellota grades and separates Spanish chorizo from Mexican before a guest orders the wrong one. The French Charcuterie is pâté and terrine cut with a hot wet knife, boudin noir explained to a hesitant table, and the foie gras order handled without improvising. Central Europe, America and the Wider Cure places Black Forest ham, the kielbasa family and country ham's salt. Read How It Was Cured (Reference) last: it answers the nitrite question without a myth, and tells you when to hand it to the chef.

What Is in the Bottle stands apart from the boards: for any well or call order, what the spirit is made from, roughly what it tastes like and what it substitutes for. The level page opens three doors: the first module, the track of all 27 modules, and Drill, over this level's modules with the whole track as the field. A module is met through its terms: every term recalled met or close in the drill. So take one module, then the drill, and move on when none of its terms is missed. The Level test at the foot of the page is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers.

primers.lede: Project dishes, two from the fire and the rest from the capstone, that cook for a room rather than a plate and run from one hour to a twelve-hour day.
paragraphs: None of the dishes at Chef is a plate you put up between tickets. Two come from Fire & Smoke: Tacos al Pastor (Home Trompo) and Central Texas Smoked Brisket, the semester where live fire is the ingredient and the cook is counted in hours. Four come from The Restaurateur's Capstone, the final semester that cooks for a room, not a plate: Sauce Espagnole & Demi-Glace, Dry-Brined Roast Turkey with Real Gravy, Salt-Baked Whole Fish and Baked Alaska. What they share is not one technique but a plan: all but the fish ask you to schedule the day and hold a standard over a long wait, and two are finished in front of people.

Take Salt-Baked Whole Fish first. It is the shortest here at an hour and the only one at difficulty 2, and it teaches you to trust a method you cannot see into: the fish steams inside its crust and you judge it by time for its weight, or by a probe pushed through the crust, not by looking. Next take Sauce Espagnole & Demi-Glace, because it is the base a brown-sauce station stands on: a roux, seared bones, then hours of skimming and reducing until the sauce coats a spoon. It is the mother sauce Chef de Partie named and this level makes at scale.

Then the holiday bird and the theater dessert. Dry-Brined Roast Turkey with Real Gravy is the bird: the salt goes on a day or more ahead, it roasts in a hot oven, and the gravy is built from the drippings and passed through a sieve so it arrives clean. Baked Alaska is a dessert made to be seen: a meringue whipped stiff enough to insulate the ice cream and cake beneath it, then browned fast. Both are cooked for a table that is watching.

Leave the two fire dishes for days you own from morning to night. Tacos al Pastor (Home Trompo) is four hours: the marinade of acid, salt and time does its work before the stack goes near the heat, then the stack roasts in a hot oven and the slices are seared hard on the plancha as you carve. Central Texas Smoked Brisket is twelve. Low and slow smoking carries the dish, with a wrapped braise through the middle hours, and the last two steps, resting the meat and slicing against the grain, are where most briskets are lost. Cook the pastor before the brisket: it roasts in the oven and finishes on the plancha, a plate you can put up in one day before you give twelve hours to the smoker.

The doors pick the next dish for you. Read the semester opens the Path of Study at the semester teaching the first dish you have not cooked, so start there and read the whole semester before you shop. Cook the next dish takes you straight to that recipe page. The library at this level shows the grid filtered to this difficulty when you want your own order. A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged: cooked once, honestly, and written down. Nothing else is asked of it.
